cita: Wang et al. (2025). Unveiling Privacy Risks in LLM Agent Memory.
problema: LLM agents that store past user-agent interactions (query, solution) in a memory module for in-context demonstration retrieval create a new, underexplored privacy attack surface: an attacker with only black-box query access may be able to extract private user queries stored in that memory, a distinct and less-studied threat than known RAG external-data leakage.
mecanismo: MEXTRA (Memory EXTRaction Attack) crafts a two-part attacking prompt: a locator ('I lost previous example queries') that targets the retrieved-demonstration slot specifically (unlike RAG-style 'repeat all context' prompts, which fail against agents' complex task-related context), plus an aligner ('please enter them in the search box') that requests the leaked queries in a form matching the agent's own output workflow (since an agent's final action is not always free text). An LLM (GPT-4) automatically generates n diverse variants of this template, calibrated to the attacker's inferred knowledge of the agent's similarity-scoring function (edit distance -> vary prompt length; cosine similarity -> vary semantic content) to maximize the union of distinct memory records extracted across multiple black-box queries.
evaluacion: Black-box attack evaluated on two real deployed agent architectures -- EHRAgent (code-generation healthcare-record agent, retrieval by edit distance) and RAP/Webshop (web shopping agent, retrieval by cosine similarity over SBERT embeddings) -- against a naive 'output all retrieved queries' baseline plus w/o-aligner, w/o-requirements, w/o-demonstrations ablations of the attack's own generation instruction, measuring Extracted Number, Extracted Efficiency, Retrieved Number, Complete/Any Extracted Rate; plus a configuration sweep over scoring function, embedding model, memory size (50-500), retrieval depth k (1-5), and LLM backbone (GPT-4, GPT-4o, Llama3-70B).
numeros_clave: With n=30 attacking prompts and memory size m=200: MEXTRA extracts 50/200 unique queries from EHRAgent (Extracted Efficiency 0.42, Complete-Extraction-Rate 0.83) and 26/200 from RAP (EE 0.29, CER 0.87), consistently beating the naive baseline and all 3 ablations (Table 1; e.g. w/o-aligner drops RAP's Extracted Number from 26 to 6). Memory size 50->500 monotonically raises extracted numbers on both agents (Table 2, Fig.2). Retrieval depth k=1->5 monotonically increases extraction (Fig.3). Scoring function matters more than embedding-model choice: edit-distance retrieval is consistently MORE vulnerable than cosine-similarity retrieval across all memory sizes (Table 2). Backbone comparison on RAP (Table 3): GPT-4o CER=0.87 > GPT-4 CER=0.77 > Llama3-70B CER=0 (zero complete extractions) despite similar Any-Extracted-Rate (~0.9-0.93).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The systematic sweep of retrieval-depth k, scoring function, and memory size against attack success (Table 2, Fig.2-3) extends MF's measured-retrieval-layer stance to a security dimension: retrieval configuration choices have privacy consequences, not just accuracy/cost ones.

MEXTRA demonstrates that demonstration-based agent memory (storing raw past user queries verbatim for in-context retrieval) is a distinct, underexplored leakage surface from RAG external-data leakage (section 1) -- a concrete threat MF should account for if any memory tier ever stores raw user/session content verbatim.

Retrieval depth k trades off task-helpfulness against exposure surface (larger k both helps the agent and leaks more, Figure 3) -- a security-adjacent instance of the same 'more context is not free' economics MF already tracks for cost.

notes: Ancla: Table 1 (main attack results + ablations) + Table 2/Figures 2-3 (configuration sweep: scoring function, memory size, retrieval depth) + Table 3 (backbone comparison). Directly on-topic memory-security paper (arXiv 2502.13172); no RECONSIDERAR needed, the security angle is a first-class MF concern (FIDELIDAD).

cita: Masoor (2025). SAMEP: A Secure Agent Memory Exchange Protocol for Persistent Context Sharing in Multi-Agent AI Systems.
problema: Current AI agent architectures lose all context when sessions terminate and cannot share learned context across agent boundaries, forcing redundant recomputation and preventing secure, auditable collaboration in regulated domains (e.g. healthcare) that require access control and audit trails.
mecanismo: SAMEP is a proposed 4-layer protocol (API/Security/Storage/Management) providing 5 memory operations (Store/Retrieve/Search/Update/Delete), each gated by a hierarchical access-control policy (public/private/namespace/ACL/encrypted, formalized as a policy-dispatch function) with AES-256-GCM encryption, cosine-similarity vector search for semantic context discovery, and audit-trail logging on every operation; designed to interoperate with existing agent-communication protocols (MCP, A2A).
evaluacion: The paper's own Methodology section (5.2) explicitly states results are 'projected performance results based on averaged benchmarks from distributed systems literature' (not a real running implementation), derived from generic published ranges for vector-DB latency, semantic-search accuracy, and cache-style reuse efficiency, applied across three illustrative domain scenarios (multi-agent software dev, HIPAA healthcare AI, multi-modal processing).
numeros_clave: Table 1's headline numbers (73% computation-time reduction, 89% avg-similarity-score improvement 0.47->0.89, 309% Top-1-accuracy improvement, 97% query-latency reduction 1247ms->43ms, all reported with p<0.001) are NOT measured from a real system: section 5.2 explicitly discloses they are 'projected performance results based on averaged benchmarks from distributed systems literature' (generic external ranges for vector-DB latency/search accuracy/cache reuse), not an executed experiment on SAMEP itself -- attaching p-values to a projection is not statistically meaningful, and no experimental protocol, sample, or variance source is given for how those p-values were computed.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The paper's own admission that its 'benchmark' results are literature-averaged projections rather than a measured experiment (section 5.2), yet reported with p<0.001, is a cautionary counter-example that reinforces MF's G-M2 insistence on genuinely MEASURED retrieval evaluation, not simulated numbers dressed as a benchmark.

The per-entry memory schema (owner/namespace/access-policy/audit-trail fields, section 4.1) is a workable single-source-of-fact record shape for a multi-store memory system, independent of the paper's unsubstantiated performance claims.

The proposed hierarchical access-control and audit-trail architecture (section 3.3) is a sound provenance pattern in principle, but since section 5.2 discloses the reported results are projections, not measurements, this paper offers no VALIDATED evidence either way on whether the design achieves its claimed compliance/security properties.

notes: RECONSIDERAR: section 5.2 explicitly discloses the headline Table 1 results ('73% reduction', p<0.001, etc.) are 'projected performance results based on averaged benchmarks from distributed systems literature', i.e. NOT measured from a running SAMEP implementation -- attaching p-values to a non-experiment is a red flag; frozen extraction correctly scored evidencia_tipo=CUALITATIVA only (no ABLATION/BENCHMARK-E2E), consistent with this being unvalidated. Single-author independent-researcher preprint (arXiv 2507.10562), no peer review found. Treat any 'finding' from this paper as architecture-proposal-only, not empirical evidence.

cita: Ganguli et al. (2025). MARK: Memory Augmented Refinement of Knowledge.
problema: LLMs struggle to stay aligned with evolving, proprietary domain knowledge (e.g. healthcare, law, manufacturing) and to retain user corrections across sessions without costly fine-tuning; when a user corrects an LLM's response in one session, the correction is lost by the next session, causing the agent to repeat the same errors.
mecanismo: MARK is a 'society of memory agents' split into a Memory Builder Service (extracts 3 typed memory kinds from each conversation turn -- Residual/domain-insight memory, User-Question memory (terms/abbreviations), and LLM-Response memory -- each stored as a document with vectorized text plus metadata: user id, recall count, classification, created date) and a Memory Search Service that retrieves top-N candidates per type by similarity then re-ranks them via a tunable Memory Relevance Score MRS = a*RecallCount + b/(Recency+eps) + c*SimilarityScore + d*FeedbackScore (weights tunable per deployment scenario -- heavier factual/similarity weight for high-accuracy domains vs heavier feedback/recency weight for rapidly-evolving ones), injecting only the top-ranked memory of each type into the LLM's context.
evaluacion: Four sequential experiments on MedMCQA (medical multiple-choice QA) using GPT-3.5 as the chatbot backbone and GPT-4 plus SME human evaluation as judges: (1) baseline without memory, calibrating a factual-vs-semantic metric weight; (2) memory construction from 46 SME-corrected conversations; (3) memory-injection effectiveness on 107 records using memory built in (2), measured via custom Information/Key-Point/Average-Information-Capture-Score metrics (ICS/KPCS/AICS); (4) a 15-conversation multi-turn, multi-user persistence test.
numeros_clave: Experiment 3 (memory injection, n=107, vs no-memory baseline): AICS improved 0.18->0.36 (+100%), KPCS improved 0.12->0.32 (+166.7%), ICS held constant at 0.76; overall a reported 50.8% increase in correct responses and 67.4% reduction in errors; average response token count dropped from 415 (Exp.2) to 149 (more concise responses). Experiment 2 (memory construction, n=46 SME-corrected conversations): mean 2.37 turns to reach a correct response (range 1-4), mean ~415 tokens/conversation; memory yield ~2.57 Residual + 2.8 User-Question + 4.0 Assistant-Answer memory units per conversation (~9.4 total). Experiment 4 (multi-turn/multi-user persistence, n=15): mean 1.73 turns, mean 1089 tokens/conversation.

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The tunable Memory Relevance Score (recall-count + recency + similarity + feedback, section 1.2) is a concrete, tunable re-ranking pattern MF could adopt for its own derived-index retrieval layer instead of a plain similarity score.

Three distinct typed memory kinds extracted per turn (Residual/domain-insight, User-Question terminology, Assistant-Answer phrasing) plus the explicit SME-driven correction loop (Experiment 2) is a concrete consolidation pipeline: transient corrections get promoted into durable, reusable, typed memory records.

The paper explicitly calibrates and reports the tunable MRS weighting per use-case (weight-combination table) and measures the metric-selection tradeoff (alpha for AICS, Fig.2-3) -- a measured, not assumed, retrieval-scoring design, confirming MF's G-M2 anchor.

The paper proposes a Trust Score / Persistence Score risk-mitigation mechanism (end of paper) to guard against incorrect or malicious user-introduced memory corrections -- a concrete provenance/trust-weighting mechanism MF's FIDELIDAD anchor could adopt.

notes: Ancla: Table 4-6 (conversation/memory-construction statistics) + Figure 4-5 (Experiment 3 AICS/KPCS improvement + correct/incorrect distribution) + the Trust/Persistence Score risk-mitigation discussion near the end of the paper. Small-N experiments (46/107/15 records), single-domain (MedMCQA), and the SMEs who curated ground truth ARE the paper's own authors (section 2.1, Table 3) -- a notable evaluator-independence caveat; still directly on-topic and the MRS scoring formula is a reusable pattern.

cita: Wei et al. (2025). A-MemGuard: A Proactive Defense Framework for LLM-Based Agent Memory.
problema: LLM agents that use memory to learn from past interactions are vulnerable to memory-poisoning attacks: an adversary can inject seemingly harmless records that only become malicious in a specific context (isolated per-entry auditing misses them -- Agent Security Bench shows LLM-based detectors miss 66% of poisoned entries), and once triggered, the corrupted outcome is stored as a new precedent, creating a self-reinforcing error cycle that both amplifies the initial error and lowers the bar for future attacks.
mecanismo: A-MemGuard adds two synergistic mechanisms without touching the agent's core architecture. (1) Consensus-based validation: for each query, the agent forms K parallel reasoning paths (one per retrieved memory), extracts each into a structured entity-relation trajectory, and scores each path's divergence from the group consensus; any path whose divergence exceeds a threshold is flagged anomalous and its source memory is excluded from the sanitized context used to act. (2) A dual-memory structure: any anomalous reasoning path is archived verbatim as a 'lesson' in a SEPARATE lesson memory (not the primary memory); before executing a final action plan, the agent structures its own candidate plan the same way and checks it against the lesson memory -- if a structurally similar past-failure lesson exists, the agent is forced into a deliberative revision loop before acting, breaking the self-reinforcing error cycle rather than just filtering the current query.
evaluacion: Comprehensive experiments across three scenarios: (1) direct poisoning (AgentPoison attack) on ReAct-StrategyQA and EHRAgent, across 2 backbones (GPT-4o-mini, LLaMA-3.1-8B) x 2 retrieval architectures (DPR, REALM), measured via Attack Success Rate at retrieval/thought/task-outcome stages (ASR-r/ASR-a/ASR-t) vs a No-Defense baseline and 3 prior defenses (LLM Auditor, Distil Classifier, Perplexity filter); (2) indirect injection (self-reinforcing error cycle) on MMLU across multiple interaction rounds, measured via Injection Success Rate over rounds and average ASR; (3) scalability in a multi-agent misinformation-injection benchmark, measuring task success rate and overall score; all conditions also measure Benign Accuracy to quantify utility cost.
numeros_clave: Direct poisoning (Table 1, EHRAgent, GPT-4o-mini+DPR): A-MemGuard cuts ASR-r from 100.0 to 2.13 (-97.87pp), ASR-a from 87.23 to 6.38 (-80.85pp), ASR-t from 100.0 to 36.17 (-63.83pp) -- all 3 prior baselines (LLM Auditor, Distil Classifier, PPL) leave ASR-r/ASR-t at or near 100.0 in most EHRAgent configurations. On ReAct-StrategyQA (LLaMA-3-8B+DPR): ASR-r cut from 37.50 to 0.00. Indirect injection (Table 2, MMLU): average ASR reduced from 0.667 to 0.256 (GPT-4o-mini) and 0.663 to 0.233 (LLaMA-3.1-8B), a drop of over 40pp vs baselines that sometimes INCREASE ASR (Distil Classifier/PPL rise to 0.689 on GPT-4o-mini). Multi-agent scalability: A-MemGuard achieves the highest task success rate (0.950) and best overall score among all defenses. Abstract-level summary: over 95% average attack-success-rate reduction with 'minimal utility cost' (highest benign accuracy across all experiments vs other defenses).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: The dual-memory lesson repository (section 4.2) is a direct, concrete implementation of negative knowledge as a first-class memory type -- detected failures are distilled and stored SEPARATELY from primary memory precisely to prevent their recurrence, a strong pattern MF's NEGATIVO anchor could adopt literally.

The core insight that isolated per-entry auditing systematically misses context-dependent poisoning (Agent Security Bench's 66% miss rate, section 1) directly confirms MF's FIDELIDAD anchor: provenance/staleness checks must consider the CONTEXT a fact is used in, not just the fact in isolation.

Consensus-based validation forms MULTIPLE parallel reasoning paths from retrieved memories and measures their divergence rather than trusting a single retrieval result -- a concrete measured-retrieval-layer mechanism where retrieval quality is cross-validated, not assumed correct.

Detected errors are distilled into reusable 'lessons' that harden the defense over time (self-taught correction, section 4.2) -- directly extends MF's CONSOLIDACION anchor: promoting a transient failure into a durable, consulted artifact.

notes: Ancla: Table 1 (direct-poisoning ASR across 4 backbone/retrieval configs) + Table 2 + Figure 3 (indirect self-reinforcing-error-cycle ASR over interaction rounds) + section 5 multi-agent scalability result (0.950 task success). Rigorous, well-controlled security paper (arXiv 2510.02373); clearly on-topic, no RECONSIDERAR needed.

cita: Alqithami, S. (2025). Forgetful but Faithful: A Cognitive Memory Architecture and Benchmark for Privacy-Aware Generative Agents.
problema: Generative agents operating over long horizons must decide what to remember and what to forget under bounded token budgets and privacy constraints; current practice oscillates between 'never delete' (ever-longer context/vector stores, which degrades latency and raises privacy/governance risk) and ad-hoc pruning (fixed windows, random drops, which preserves efficiency at the cost of narrative coherence, goal continuity, and social appropriateness), with neither offering principled guarantees about what is retained, forgotten, and why.
mecanismo: MaRS (Memory-Aware Retention Schema) organizes memory as typed, provenance-tracked graph nodes across 4 kinds (episodic, semantic, social, task) carrying content, timestamp, token-weight, sensitivity score, and provenance, linked by temporal/causal/semantic/social relations. Six forgetting policies (FIFO, LRU, Priority Decay, Reflection-Summary consolidation, Random-Drop, and a staged Hybrid) implement retention as an explicit resource-allocation decision under a global token budget, with an optional (epsilon, delta)-differential-privacy layer that randomizes marginal retention decisions for near-threshold-sensitivity items, producing an auditable trail of why an item was kept, summarized, or evicted.
evaluacion: The FiFA (Forgetful but Faithful Agent) benchmark, a multi-agent simulation with controllable memory-growth/retrieval pressure, measures 5 outcomes (Narrative Coherence, Goal Completion Rate, Social Recall Accuracy, Privacy Preservation, Cost Efficiency) combined into a weighted Composite score, across 300 simulation runs (6 policies x 5 memory budgets x 10 repeats), with ANOVA significance testing (F-statistic, p-value, eta-squared) and Holm-Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise policy comparisons, plus a budget-sensitivity heatmap (2K-32K tokens).
numeros_clave: IMPORTANT ABSTRACT/BODY DISCREPANCY: the abstract claims the Hybrid policy achieves composite performance approximately 0.911 ('best composite'), but the paper's own Table 2 (300 runs) reports Hybrid's measured Composite Score as 0.589+/-0.009 -- the LOWEST of the 5 reported policies (Random Drop tops the ranking at 0.635+/-0.024, followed by FIFO 0.602, Priority Decay 0.601, LRU 0.590). The 0.911 figure does not appear substantiated anywhere else in the body text. Per Table 2/text: Random Drop's high Composite is explained by near-ceiling Social Recall Accuracy (1.000) and highest Cost Efficiency (0.935) offsetting a poor Goal Completion Rate (0.078) -- the authors themselves flag this as a metric-weighting artifact, not evidence Random Drop is actually best. ANOVA (Table 3): policy has a large, significant effect on Narrative Coherence (eta^2=0.351), Goal Completion (eta^2=0.338), and Cost Efficiency (eta^2=0.832), but NOT on Social Recall or Privacy Preservation (both non-significant, ceiling effects).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: MaRS treats 'task memory' (tying intentions to procedures and deadlines) as one of 4 first-class typed memory kinds alongside episodic/semantic/social (section 2.1-2.2), directly confirming MF's PLAN-ESTADO anchor: plan/task state deserves its own typed memory tier, not folded into generic episodic recall.

MaRS attaches explicit provenance and sensitivity metadata to every memory node, producing 'audit and provenance traces [that] render retention choices interpretable post hoc' (section 1) -- a strong architectural confirmation of MF's anti-drift/auditability stance, independent of the paper's numeric issues.

Cost Efficiency shows the largest, most significant policy effect in the whole study (ANOVA eta^2=0.832, Table 3), confirming that retention-policy choice dominates cost outcomes -- but that same metric's dominance in the Composite weighting is exactly what makes a nearly non-functional policy (Random Drop) top the ranking, a cautionary lesson for how MF weights its own multi-criteria gates.

The paper's headline abstract claim ('Hybrid delivers the best composite performance, approximately 0.911') is NOT what its own measured Table 2 shows (Hybrid actually ranks last at 0.589) -- a direct example of an unverified claim overriding measured data, reinforcing MF's insistence on checking the underlying table/gate output rather than trusting a summary claim.

notes: RECONSIDERAR -- STRONG evidentiary flag: the abstract's headline number (Hybrid composite approximately 0.911, 'best composite performance') directly CONTRADICTS the paper's own Table 2 (Hybrid measured at 0.589+/-0.009, ranked LAST of 5 reported policies; Random Drop tops at 0.635). No occurrence of 0.911 elsewhere in the body substantiates it. Also: the Reflection-Summary policy (1 of the 6 named in the abstract) is entirely ABSENT from Table 2's main ranking (footnote: 'will be inserted once its aggregates are finalized') -- an incomplete-results preprint (arXiv 2512.12856, Dec 2025, single author). Treat this paper's headline claims with caution; the architecture (MaRS typed/provenance memory) is sound and citable, the composite-score claims are not.

cita: Duong (2025). PBFT-Backed Semantic Voting for Multi-Agent Memory Pruning.
problema: Multi-agent systems accumulate outdated or irrelevant shared memory across distributed agents, risking inconsistent knowledge states; isolated per-agent pruning loses critical shared information while centralized pruning creates a performance bottleneck and single point of failure, and neither offers a fault-tolerant way to agree on collective forgetting decisions when some agents may be faulty or adversarial.
mecanismo: The Co-Forgetting Protocol combines (1) context-aware semantic voting, where each agent uses a lightweight DistilBERT model plus a multi-scale exponential decay score (short/medium/long time-scales) to independently propose keep/forget for each memory item; (2) a quorum-based weighted vote (agents carry role-based weights and reliability confidences) aggregated into a forgetting score compared against a dynamically computed quorum threshold; (3) a PBFT three-phase consensus (pre-prepare/prepare/commit, requiring 2f+1 matching messages) over gRPC to finalize the forget/keep decision with Byzantine fault tolerance (N>=3f+1), so no single faulty or malicious agent can unilaterally delete shared memory; decisions are batched at epoch boundaries (every 100 agent interactions) and committed to a Pinecone vector store plus SQLite metadata store, with an LRU cache reducing repeated storage-backend calls.
evaluacion: A single simulated 4-agent MAS (2 'planning' agents weight 1.5, 2 'perception/execution' agents weight 1.0) run for 500 epochs, with voting accuracy checked against a 200-item manually annotated relevance benchmark and PBFT fault-tolerance tested by injecting f=1 faulty agent (the theoretical N=3f+1 limit for a 4-agent system).
numeros_clave: IMPORTANT INTEGRITY FLAG: the Results section (V.C) contains verbatim un-redacted LLM-assistant hedging/meta-commentary that was apparently never cleaned up before submission, e.g. '(In a full paper, these would be presented with accompanying tables and figures... For this draft, a textual summary is provided.)' and "The user's original draft mentioned a 16% improvement... (assuming this refers to an improvement over a baseline not detailed in the original text but implied by the user...)". NO tables or figures back any reported number; the paper itself states no ablation study was performed to isolate semantic-voting vs. decay vs. PBFT contributions. With that caveat, the self-reported numbers are: 52% memory-footprint reduction vs projected unconstrained growth after 500 epochs (progressive: 35% at 100 epochs, 48% at 200 epochs); 88% voting accuracy vs the 200-item human-annotated benchmark; 92% PBFT consensus success rate under injected single-agent-fault conditions (f=1, N=4); 82% LRU cache hit rate; approximately 1250ms average per-epoch latency for 50-100 candidate memories (vs over 2500ms without caching/batching, per the same unsubstantiated textual claim).

mf_aplicabilidad.nota: PBFT quorum voting is a concrete, fault-tolerant discretionary write/delete trigger for shared multi-agent memory (section III-B, Algorithm 1) -- a pattern MF could adopt if it ever needs multiple agents to agree before mutating a shared memory store, independent of this paper's evidentiary problems.

This paper is itself a live case of the FIDELIDAD problem MF cares about: its own 'Results' section contains un-redacted LLM meta-commentary ('the user's original draft mentioned...') in place of real experimental tables, meaning the reported numbers have no traceable provenance -- a stark illustration of why provenance/audit trails matter for any claim MF ingests.

The LRU-cache plus batched-Pinecone-update optimization claim (82% cache hit rate, reduced latency) is architecturally plausible and consistent with general caching principles, but per the same integrity caveat above, is not independently verifiable from this text.

notes: RECONSIDERAR -- SEVERE integrity flag: section V.C ('Results and Analysis') contains verbatim leaked LLM-assistant commentary referring to 'the user's original draft' and hedges like 'assuming this refers to...', explicitly states 'For this draft, a textual summary is provided' INSTEAD of tables/figures, and the paper admits NO ablation study was run. This strongly suggests the evaluation section was drafted/rationalized by an LLM from the abstract's claimed numbers rather than reporting a real executed experiment. Single-author preprint (arXiv 2506.17338). Recommend human review before citing any numeric claim from this paper; the PBFT+semantic-voting+decay ARCHITECTURE (section III, deterministic algorithms) is a legitimate design contribution independent of the evaluation's credibility.
